articles.fullContent:
At some point, someone on your team has probably asked, “Should we be on Bluesky?” 

Whether you’re ready to go all-in or just test the waters, it helps to know what you’re getting into first.

Here’s everything you need to know about Bluesky, plus a step-by-step guide to building a strategy that works.

Key takeaways

  1. Bluesky is big enough to experiment with. It grew nearly 60% in 2025, and now has over 46 million users.
  2. You can’t buy reach. Bluesky has no ads, so attention has to come from useful posts and real conversations.
  3. Bluesky has custom feeds. Users choose their own feeds, so there’s no single algorithm to game.
  4. Consistency matters more than usual. Bluesky’s Following feed is chronological, so posts get buried quickly. A steady, realistic schedule keeps you visible.
  5. Tools like Hootsuite keep Bluesky manageable. Schedule posts with Perch, track conversations with Lumen, and ask Wisdom what’s working.

What is Bluesky, and why does it need its own strategy?

Bluesky is a decentralized social network where people share short posts, follow accounts, and choose their own feeds. It looks a lot like early Twitter, but with one big difference: users have more control over their experience.

Bluesky needs its own strategy for a few reasons:

  • There’s no single algorithm to game. Most social platforms are ruled by algorithms. On Bluesky, users can pick and choose their feeds, which makes “cracking the algorithm” a less effective strategy.
  • You can’t buy reach. Bluesky is ad-free, so brands can’t buy their way into people’s feeds. If you want attention, you have to earn it organically.
  • Discovery is different: Bluesky is home to hundreds of niche communities. The trick is finding the ones that matter to your audience, then showing up often enough to become a familiar name.

How does Bluesky differ from algorithmic platforms?

On most social platforms, an algorithm decides what you see and when. Bluesky gives that control back to users. 

With customizable feeds, users can follow specific topics or interests (like gardening or astronomy) without relying on a single algorithm to determine what appears in their timeline. Anyone can create a feed, and users can pin their favorites right to their home screen.

Why are brands paying attention to Bluesky now?

Brands are paying attention to Bluesky because it’s big enough to matter, but still early enough to stand out. It’s also become a hub for journalists, researchers, and industry experts, which makes it a natural fit for thought leadership. And since there are no ads, every brand starts on equal footing, no matter the size of its budget.

Key Takeaways

  • SEO templates save time by giving you repeatable frameworks for everything from keyword planning, audits, reporting, content creation, outreach, and local SEO.
  • The best templates act as starting points, not shortcuts. You’ll get the most out of them by customizing around your goals and audience, instead of copying them exactly.
  • Free tools like Ubersuggest and downloadable spreadsheets can simplify diagnostic tasks (like technical checks or backlink analysis) and tracking (such as keyword or performance reporting).
  • Content-focused templates help you plan, write, edit, and publish more consistently by turning scattered ideas into clear briefs, calendars, outlines, and checklists.
  • With search changing, templates should help you track how your brand appears in AI-generated answers as well as traditional search results.

Tired of spending tons of time building SEO spreadsheets, sorting data, and double-checking each step? I’ve put together 19 SEO templates to make your life easier. 

From tracking organic traffic to writing the perfect blog post, these resources cover every step of the SEO process. I’ve also included an AI visibility template, because ranking on Google is no longer the full story.

Each template is a starting point you can customize to fit your goals and your workflow.

1. Google Data Studio Overall Traffic Report Template

Google Data Studio lets you connect, visualize, and share your data in one place. Use it to build interactive dashboards and reports that turn raw data into decisions your team can act on.

It connects to hundreds of data sources, including:

  • Looker by Google
  • Google Analytics and Sheets
  • PayPal
  • HubSpot
  • QuickBooks
  • Salesforce

Source: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/looker-studio-is-data-studio

Learn more about using Data Studio for reporting here.

2. All-In-One Google Search Console Template

Analyze keywords and page views with Data Studio’s All-in-One Search Console template. It gives you a full traffic overview: brand vs. generic keywords, page rankings, keyword analysis, and total performance over time.

Within each category, you can sort by date and dig deeper to compare improved and declining keywords, analyse short-tail vs long-tail query performance, and filter results by device or country. Then share the data with your team and other collaborators. 

You’ll need to complete the setup of Google Data Studio before you can add in your site’s data.

3. NP Digital SEO Audit Guide

My detailed website audit guide walks you through:

  • Tightening your titles and descriptions, since Google often rewrites meta descriptions
  • Stopping keyword cannibalization and duplicating content by consolidating pages
  • Filling content gaps your competitors are winning
  • Cleaning up your structured data and schema so AI Overviews can cite you
  • Building experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T) with credentialed authors and original data.

articles.title: Week of Oct. 5 Cable News Ratings: CNN Up in Both Measurements
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of October 5, 2026.

CNN, which in recent weeks has been in the news because of the White House press ban and its new ownership situation, stood tall among its competitors, finishing the week as the only one with gains in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

The now-Skydance network closed the demo between it and MS NOW during total day, leaving a difference of only 1,000 viewers between the two networks.

MS NOW was the only network with across-the-board declines, but it also had some positive news. In the 9 p.m. ET hour, The Rachel Maddow Show was the most-watched show in total viewers on Monday, October 5. It was also the most-watched network in both measured categories during the 6 a.m. ET hour, when Morning Joe airs on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.

As for Fox News, its bright spot was its primetime demo growth during the just-concluded week. It’s still the most-watched network by a large margin.

NETWORKS: According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Oct. 5, Fox News averaged 1.6 million total viewers and 145,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network was down -2% in total viewers but grew by +4% in the demo compared to the prior week ( the week beginning Sept. 28 ).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.07 million total viewers and 94,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on its average from the previous week’s measurements, the network was flat in total viewers and the demo.

Fox News dropped from second to third place in total primetime viewership and was sixth in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and finished in fifth place in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 902,000 total viewers and 88,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network was down -2% in total viewers and -1% in the demo compared with its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 570,000 total viewers and 57,000 demo viewers. It was down -1% in total viewers and -8% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week—the only network with declines in this comparison.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW slipped from third to fifth place in total primetime viewers and was 15th in the demo, tied with Comedy Central. It also ranked third in total viewers and finished in eighth place in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 577,000 total primetime viewers and 100,000 demo viewers. It grew by +4% in total viewers and +3% in the demo compared to the previous week.

During total day, the network had 393,000 total viewers and 56,000 viewers in the demo. For CNN, this represented gains of +7% in total viewers and +8% in the demo during this daypart.

Among all cable networks, CNN moved from seventh to sixth place in total viewers and was 11th in the demo during primetime. It slipped to No. 5 in total day among total viewers and was ninth in the demo.

When looking at these networks’ performance during the same period a year ago :

During primetime, Fox News was down -30% in total viewers and -34% in the A25-54 demo. During total day, the network was down -28% in total viewers and -35% in the demo.

MS NOW was up +11% in total viewers and +13% in the demo. During total day, the network gained +13% in total viewers and +24% in the demo—the only network with gains in both measured categories in this yearly comparison.

In primetime, CNN was up by +26% in total viewers and +52% in the demo. During total day, it was up by +3% in total viewers and flat in the demo.

PROGRAMMING: Fox News held 12 of the 15 spots among the week’s most-watched cable news shows, with The Five in first place with 2.649 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW was represented in the chart by Monday’s 9 p.m. ET airing of The Rachel Maddow Show, with 1.779 million total viewers at No. 6. The Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell , airing weeknights at 10 p.m. ET, had 1.122 million total viewers at No. 14, and The Briefing with Jen Psaki , airing Tuesday to Friday at 9 p.m., was in the No. 15 position, with 1.078 million total viewers.

The Rachel Maddow Show dethroned The Five to take the top spot in the Adults 25-54 demo, with 252,000 viewers. Despite this, Fox News held 12 of the 15 top spots in the demo, with The Five averaging 239,000 viewers to take second place. CNN was represented by CNN NewsNight with Abby Phillip , which airs five nights a week at 10 p.m. ET and finished in eighth place with 144,000 viewers, and The Source with Kaitlan Collins , which airs weeknights at 9 p.m. ET, and finished in 14th place with 116,000 demo viewers.

articles.fullContent:
In It Was There a Minute Ago , I mentioned that reading research papers had become something of a hobby … It’s borderline masochism. I’ve kept going, working through papers and white papers and trying to connect the dots between experiments. What interests me is how a finding in one study changes the way I read another.

Last time, I looked at what a missing answer lets us diagnose. This time, I want to look at the apparent success: The model seems to have learned the material, and we are ready to congratulate ourselves.

A model can become extremely good at predicting the facts in a biography and still struggle when you ask where the person works. Researchers documented that gap . The reading had gone very well. The questions were a bit of a problem.

Think of a pupil who can recite a passage from the textbook, right up to the punctuation. Ask a question that requires taking a fact out of that passage and the performance changes. We would probably want to see the exam results before declaring the revision a success.

That is the distinction I keep pointing to when people talk about getting a brand into model memory . The phrase makes the difficult part sound finished. Once the model has encountered your name during training, it is supposed to know you well enough for the recommendations to follow. Very efficient, if that is all it takes.

Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1 uses fictional biographies to separate memorizing text from extracting its facts. The researchers pre-trained small models on the biographies, then fine-tuned them on questions about some people and tested questions about the others.

Here, pre-training means learning from the biographies from scratch; fine-tuning is the subsequent training on the question-answer task. Both change the model’s learned parameters, or weights. Information it can use from those weights, without fetching a source, is what we mean here by parametric memory .

The model had seen each test person’s biography, but had never been trained on questions about that person. Failure cannot be waved away as never having received the material.

The pupil comparison helps with the difference between recitation and answering. It tells us nothing about whether a model understands something in the human sense. The question is whether it can use facts learned in one form to answer questions asked in another.

A model that completes your product description, when given the beginning, has passed a particular test. A buyer asking which product suits their needs has set it another. I would be cautious about a memory claim that slides between them without saying so.

The obvious response is more repetition. Give it the lesson again, until it sticks.

In Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models , duplication in the training corpus increases verbatim extraction: supply the beginning of a training passage and the model becomes more likely to reproduce the continuation.

So, the comfortable counterclaim, that copies teach a model nothing, is too broad. Repetition can improve a measured result. The question is: Which result?

A newer paper, Don’t Forget! Decomposing the Training Dynamics of Memorization in Language Models , asks what happens to a memorized passage as training continues. The researchers used saved versions of Pythia models to simulate training updates, changes to their learned weights.

In those simulations, learning from other data worked more strongly against predicting frequently repeated memorized passages than rare ones, especially in the model with one billion parameters. The researchers suggest that repetition may help keep those passages reproducible despite that interference.

They did not vary repetition and the competing training data separately to prove that explanation. And they tested word-for-word continuation, not answers about the facts.

Coming back to our analogy, the pupil also has the rest of the syllabus to contend with. A mention count cannot tell you how learning from other material affects the result you want.

Being able to finish the passage still leaves open whether the model can use its facts to answer a different kind of question. More successful recitation cannot settle that on its own. Nor is a repeated publication automatically a repeated training exposure. The model provider still has to collect the copy , keep it after filtering and actually use it in training.

I can see why counting mentions appeals. You can count them before you know what they will teach.

In the biography experiment, the researchers varied the wording, shuffled sentence order, and repeated each person’s full name throughout their biography. Accuracy on factual questions about the test group rose from 9.7% to 96.2% in a 124-million-parameter GPT-2 model. Those were synthetic facts in a small-model training experiment, not commercial brand recommendations.

The result gives me a better way to think about a brand fact than simply asking how often the sentence appears. Consider an invented payments company. One description explains how its payout feature helps marketplace sellers; another explains how the same feature handles a customer’s payment problem. The descriptions concern the same product, but could help answer different questions.

That gives me a reason to test clear descriptions of a product in different situations. It does not tell me that publishing those descriptions will make a commercial model remember the product better.

The researchers chose their training material and trained the model on it themselves. A publisher can put pages online, but the model provider decides whether those pages enter training , which copies to keep, and how to use them.

If you use that result to sell a package of webpages , you are promising an improvement the researchers never tested. Putting the paper in the proposal does not fill that gap.

Better descriptions could still help. I would want evidence that the publishing work improved recall before promising it to a client. And the large gain in this small biography model does not tell us what improvement to expect from a much larger commercial model.

The researchers also kept one group’s biographies unchanged while adding varied biographies for another group. Accuracy on questions about the unchanged group rose from 4.4% to 86.8% .

For the later question-answer training, they used examples about only the added group. The test group’s biographies had not gained extra versions, and its question-answer pairs were never used in training. Training on material about other people had helped the model answer questions about this group. The transfer depended on sufficiently similar material.

Back in the classroom, the pupil gets better at using a lesson because the teaching has improved elsewhere. Their own passage has not acquired another paragraph.

This is the finding that makes a neat brand-content explanation feel incomplete to me. The quality of everything written about a brand may matter. So may the model’s ability to use information of that kind, developed through training on other examples.

If similar transfer matters for commercial facts, your brand could become easier to recall after a model change without anyone having rewritten your brand material. That is a hypothesis about production systems, not a result these researchers measured.

articles.title: Brandweek 2026: Does ROAS Tell the Whole Story? ft. Jason Pirock
articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026 , Jenny Rooney sits down with Jason Pirock, former vice president of global brand marketing at Outrigger Resorts and Hotels, to discuss why differentiation may be one of marketing’s most underhyped priorities right now.

Jason challenges the industry’s fixation on ROAS and reveals why CXO titles don’t matter as much as you’d think.

He also discusses why landing a creator with a huge following can mean very little if the partnership wasn’t designed the right way.

Finally, Jason touches on why hospitality traditionally lags behind other industries when it comes to technology, and why it’s catching up now.

Why hospitality’s adoption of AI is accelerating after years of lagging behind other industries

Why consumers are gravitating back toward real-world experiences and human interaction

Why authentic creator fit matters more than reach or follower count

Why senior marketing titles matter less than alignment with leadership

Why ROAS should be treated as a directional indicator rather than the full definition of success

How a builder mindset can shape a marketing leader’s career

Why differentiation becomes even more important as AI makes generic execution easier

This episode is part of a special vidcast series that was recorded live during Brandweek 2026 and presented in partnership with Tatari.

Jason Pirock is the former VP of global brand marketing at Outrigger Resorts and Hotels, with nearly 20 years of experience across retail, commercial real estate, and hospitality. His career has spanned work across Hyatt, Aparium Hotel Group, Springboard, and Outrigger.

Across those roles, Jason has consistently gravitated toward building and rebuilding, from rethinking an early business at Target to putting content creators into local markets before “creator” became standard marketing language. His perspective combines brand strategy, experiential marketing and a strong belief that differentiation matters even more as technology makes execution easier.

[04:03] Hospitality’s AI Catch-Up Is Happening Fast — Jason says hospitality has traditionally been well behind industries like retail when it comes to technology adoption. That gap is narrowing quickly. Over the past year or two, he has seen a wave of new technology companies and faster AI adoption across the sector. Much of it remains behind the scenes for now, but Jason expects more guest-facing applications to emerge, raising the stakes for brands deciding where technology genuinely improves the experience.

[09:10] Stop Choosing Creators for Reach Alone — Jason does not believe the biggest creator is automatically the best creator. The real question is whether that person already likes the brand, understands what it stands for and can create something that feels natural. For him, creator marketing should be treated like any other serious partnership: do the homework, look for mutual fit, and make sure the relationship makes sense both ways. A large audience means very little if the partnership itself feels random.

[11:17] The CMO Title Debate Is Missing the Point — CMO. CGO. CXO. Chief experience officer. Chief revenue officer. Jason thinks marketers are spending too much energy debating titles and too little on the thing that actually matters: alignment. If the CEO, board and marketing leader agree on the objectives and what success looks like, the label on the org chart becomes secondary. His Brandweek 2026 point is refreshingly simple: clarity of mandate beats title inflation.

[12:01] ROAS Is Directional, Not Definitive — Jason’s unpopular marketing opinion is one he says he will argue “until I’m blue in the face”: ROAS does not equal marketing success. He sees it as a useful directional indicator, but not a complete scoreboard. That matters particularly in hospitality, where long-term brand value, loyalty and guest experience cannot always be reduced to a single short-term efficiency metric. The danger is letting the easiest number to report become the only number leadership cares about.

Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

That shift has important implications for content teams, particularly as AI changes how audiences discover and evaluate information.

The opportunity isn’t simply to produce more content with AI. Brands need systems that connect audience insights, human expertise, content creation, distribution, and performance measurement. The teams that build these processes can continuously improve their content while adapting to changing audience behavior and search environments.

articles.title: How Websites Are Becoming a Key Trust Signal for Consumers
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

A consumer might discover a company through an AI recommendation, social platform, or traditional search result. Before making a purchase or contacting the business, they may visit its website to confirm that the company exists and learn more about what it offers.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

A professional domain, clear business information, useful content, customer reviews, and evidence of expertise can all contribute to website trust. These signals help answer a basic question that becomes increasingly important as AI-generated information becomes easier to produce: Is this business real?

AI Search Is Changing Discovery, Not Replacing Websites

The Wix report found that AI platforms are increasingly interacting with websites. Its data shows that LLMs still account for less than 1% of website traffic, although traffic from LLMs grew fourfold between 2024 and 2025.

Traditional search remains much more significant. Search accounts for 42% of traffic to Wix sites, compared with 40% from direct traffic and 13% from social.

This puts the current state of discovery into perspective. AI search is growing quickly, but traditional search continues to be a major source of website visits.

For brands, that means the website still needs to serve both audiences: people arriving directly or through search and AI systems looking for information to use in their responses.

What the Wix Data Says About Website Trust

The report highlights several website characteristics associated with stronger business performance.


Source

Structured Data Can Support Visibility

One of the clearest findings concerns structured data.

Wix found that sites with structured data markup that passed Google’s rich-results inspection earned 2x more revenue and received 9x more traffic than sites without it.

This is a correlation in Wix’s dataset, not evidence that adding structured data directly causes those outcomes. Still, the finding reinforces the importance of making website information easier for search engines and AI systems to understand.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

For brands investing in AI visibility, technical foundations such as structured data should therefore remain part of the conversation.

articles.title: Building trust through social media: 5 ways to earn it
articles.fullContent:
Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey. But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.

People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.

Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.

Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.

Why trust is now built on social media first

People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.

Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:

  • Search: 21% of consumers turn to social media first when searching for information, according to Q2 data.
  • Influencer impact: 67% made a purchase directly because of an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.
  • Trends and culture: Q3 data found that 54% of consumers turn to social media to keep up with trends and cultural moments, ahead of TV and streaming at 45% and conversations with friends and family at 42%.

These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.

For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.


The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.

How building trust on social media is a growth lever

Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:

  • Authentic influencer partnerships build buying confidence. Eighty-one percent of consumers say it matters whether an influencer has used the product they promote. Creators with firsthand product experience offer more credible recommendations.
  • Employee content introduces potential customers to your business. Forty percent of consumers rated employee-generated content as more authentic than posts from a brand’s main account. The same proportion discover products or services through employee content at least once a month.
  • Timely crisis responses protect customer relationships. Response speed influences how consumers judge a brand’s public crisis response. Addressing problems promptly and following through on a solution gives customers a reason to keep doing business with you.

The signals that earn audience trust

Building audience confidence starts with how your brand shows up day to day. The table below outlines four trust builders—consistency, responsiveness, transparency and proof—and the behaviors that undermine them.

Trust builder Trust breaker Consistency: Maintain a recognizable voice and follow through on your stated values. Chase trends that clash with your identity or make promises your actions don’t support. Responsiveness: Acknowledge questions promptly and provide helpful answers or clear next steps. Ignore customer concerns or send generic replies that don’t address the issue. Transparency: Disclose relevant AI use and paid partnerships, and acknowledge mistakes. Hide sponsorships, present AI-generated content as real experiences or avoid accountability. Proof: Share customer experiences, employee expertise and recommendations from creators who know your products. Rely on unsupported claims or endorsements from people with no firsthand product experience.

Consistency

A consistent voice and posting cadence set expectations for your brand. Your values need the same follow-through: if you promote a commitment to customer care, your replies should reflect it. Maintain that reliability across everyday posts, campaigns and difficult conversations.

Responsiveness

Helpful replies show customers that you take their concerns seriously. Sprout’s Q3 pulse survey found that 38% expect a customer care response within two hours, including 14% who expect one within minutes.

For example, SpotifyCares responds to a creator’s upload problem within minutes, connects them with the right team and invites them to follow up if they run into issues.


Speed matters during crises, too, as Q2 pulse survey findings show. Acknowledge the issue promptly, explain what you know and tell people when to expect an update. The quality of your response matters as much as how quickly you send it.

Transparency

Be up front about how you create your content and what you’re promoting. That includes paid partnerships, relevant AI use and the limits of your product claims.

Sprout’s Q1 pulse survey found that 28% of consumers most want brands to stop posting AI-generated content without labels. Disclose when content is AI-generated and have a person check it for accuracy before publishing. Disclosure explains how you created it, while human review reduces the risk of publishing inaccurate information.

A social media competitor analysis is the process of looking at your competitors’ social content and activity to understand how they compare to your own performance.

  • See which platforms they’re active on

Content volume keeps climbing as 51% of content professionals now use AI to create posts, which makes differentiation harder and raises the bar for what stands out. articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. YouTube pays per ad view, not per video view, typically an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views in 2026.
  2. Your earnings per view depend on your content niche, audience location, ad type, video length, and seasonal advertiser demand.
  3. RPM (revenue per mille) shows what you actually earn after YouTube’s 45% cut, while CPM reflects what advertisers pay.
  4. Ad revenue is only one income stream. Brand deals, channel memberships, affiliate marketing, and merch can meaningfully increase total YouTube earnings.

How YouTube’s pay-per-view system works

YouTube does have a pay-per-view system, but it might not be what you’d initially think. Instead of getting paid for each video view, YouTubers are paid for each ad view.

Let’s dig a little deeper into what these two types of views mean:

  • Video views: The number of views your video gets.
  • Ad views: The number of views that ads on your video get.

YouTube pays you for the amount of ad views your video gets. If your video has a million views but no advertising on it, you won’t be making any money. If your video has a million views but only 10,000 ad views, you’ll be making money only on the 10,000 ad views.

Similarly, you might have multiple ads run within a single YouTube video. If users actually watch those ads all the way through, you could also end up with more ad views than video views.

Essentially, YouTube makes money off the advertising space, so it will only pay based on how much exposure your video generates for that advertising space. Of that advertising money, YouTube keeps 45% and you keep 55%. Through this model, YouTube has paid creators over $100 billion since 2021.

The short version: Your YouTube income is a share of ad revenue tied to ad views, not a flat rate per video view.

What are CPM, RPM, and CPC on YouTube?

CPM, RPM, and CPC are the three metrics that explain the gap between what advertisers spend and what lands in your bank account. They sound similar, but they measure very different things, and mixing them up is the fastest way to end up disappointed by your first payout.

Revenue per mille is the one worth watching. RPM is almost always lower than CPM because it accounts for YouTube’s 45% revenue share, plus all the views that never got an ad at all. A $12 CPM does not mean $12 in your pocket per 1,000 views.

So when you compare earnings numbers with other creators, check which metric they’re quoting. CPM tells you how valuable your audience is to advertisers, and RPM tells you what your channel actually earns.

How much does YouTube pay per 1,000 views in 2026?

In 2026, a YouTuber can earn an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views. This is an industry estimate rather than a published YouTube rate, and because not every video view triggers an ad, your earnings per 1,000 video views land lower than that range.

Can you make a full-time job out of being a YouTuber? Yes, but the math has to work at volume. A single 10,000-view video sitting in the middle of that estimated range brings in around $60. Publish one of those every day and you’re looking at roughly $21,900 a year, which isn’t a great salary on its own.

That assumes you stay stagnant, though. If you’re actually publishing new video content every day, or even once or twice a week, you should see compounding growth in views, subscribers, and ad revenue. And as you grow, you can layer in other monetization avenues.

articles.title: Average engagement rates for 13 industries in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A “good” engagement rate falls between 1% and 5%, but what counts as strong varies significantly by industry and platform.
  2. Instagram leads overall engagement at 4.2% across industries, followed by LinkedIn at 3.9%.
  3. Construction, education, and nonprofits consistently post the highest average engagement rates across platforms.
  4. You can calculate your engagement rate with a simple formula, or use Perch by Hootsuite to track rates and benchmark against your industry automatically.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is the percentage of your audience that interacts with a piece of content, rather than just scrolling past it. It’s calculated by dividing total interactions by a measure of audience size (usually followers, reach, or impressions), then multiplying by 100.

What counts as an interaction depends on the platform, but it typically includes:

  • Likes: The lowest-effort signal of interest
  • Comments: A stronger signal, since they take real effort
  • Shares and reposts: Content worth passing along to someone else
  • Saves: Content people want to come back to
  • Clicks: Link clicks, profile visits, or taps on your content
  • DMs: Direct replies or message shares

The key thing to remember is that engagement rate measures quality of attention relative to audience size, which is why a small account can easily outperform a much larger one.

Bonus !!!

Use our free engagement rate calculator to find out your engagement rate 4 ways fast. Calculate it on a post-by-post basis or for an entire campaign — for any social network.

Download now

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it’s one of the few social media metrics that tells you whether your content actually connected with people. Follower counts and impressions measure exposure. Engagement measures response.

For marketing leaders, tracking the social media engagement rate across accounts serves four practical purposes:

  • Content quality signal: A dip in engagement often shows up before a dip in followers or conversions, making it an early warning system for content quality problems.
  • Algorithm input: Most platforms use engagement signals to decide how widely to distribute a post, so higher engagement compounds into more reach.
  • ROI indicator: Engagement rate normalizes for audience size, which makes it a fair way to compare performance across channels, regions, or business units.
  • Strategy guide: Comparing engagement by format and topic shows you what to produce more of, and what to stop making.

In short, engagement rate is the metric that tells you whether your audience cares, not just whether they saw it.

How do you calculate engagement rate?

You calculate engagement rate by dividing total engagements by an audience measure, then multiplying by 100. Which audience measure you use depends on what you’re trying to learn. There are three common methods:

  1. Engagement rate by reach, for judging content performance among people who saw it
  2. Engagement rate by followers, for benchmarking against industry averages
  3. Engagement rate by impressions, for paid campaigns and repeat exposure

Here’s how each one works. For more variations, including daily and cost-per-engagement formulas, see our full guide to measuring social engagement.

Engagement rate by reach

Formula: (Total engagements / Reach) x 100

This is the most accurate measure of content quality, because it only counts people who actually saw the post. Use it when you want to know how compelling a piece of content was.

Engagement rate by followers

Formula: (Total engagements / Followers) x 100

This is the most widely reported engagement rate formula, and the one used for the industry benchmarks below. Use it when you need to compare your performance to published averages.

Engagement rate by impressions

You’ve heard it from mentors, recruiters and that coworker who posts on LinkedIn every morning: You need a personal brand. Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. This guide shows you how to take control of that perception and turn it into real opportunities.

Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Voice and values. That is, what you say and what you believe. Your brand voice shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all or robotic.

  • Content. What you create, and how you present it, attracts your audience. If you write long-form newsletters, mastering Substack SEO gets those deep dives discovered by new readers.

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.

Instagram verification is the process of getting a blue checkmark badge that appears next to your username on the platform. The verification badge signals to other users on the platform that an account really belongs to the user, artist, brand, or organization it represents.

If you’re looking to enhance your presence while pursuing verification, consider brainstorming unique Instagram username ideas that reflect your brand identity.

  • Impersonation protection: Fake accounts exist for all kinds of reasons, from scams to parodies. A badge sets your account apart from impersonators, and Meta Verified adds proactive account monitoring to help protect your account from impersonators or hackers.
  • Visibility and performance: Verified accounts appear at or near the top of comments and search results when people type in a business name. They also appear as a recommended business to follow in the Feed, which can translate into more followers, website clicks, and conversions.
  • Extra features: Verified accounts get access to perks like exclusive stickers on Instagram Stories and Reels to help their content stand out.

No matter which method an account used to get verified, the blue checkmark looks the same. That means it’s impossible to know whether it was awarded to a user through traditional means or if they’re paying for the Meta Verified service.

Traditional verification requirements

Instagram’s criteria is a bit vague, but here’s what we do know.

In addition to following Instagram’s Terms of Use and Community Guidelines, your account also needs to be:

  • Two-factor authentication enabled on your profile

articles.title: How Atlas Copco Group built a proactive reputation intelligence model
articles.fullContent:
Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

These signals are easy to miss when you rely on alerts alone because each one can seem too minor to warrant attention. With social intelligence, Atlas Copco Group brings those signals together to spot patterns that need a closer look before they impact business performance.

Atlas Copco Group’s 5-step reputation intelligence model

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

The model is based on five practices that help them spot emerging risk, strengthen brand presence and manage issues consistently.

1. Catch weak signals early

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

To identify which weak signals matter for your brand, start with the reputation risks you already monitor and work backward. What behaviors, questions or changes tend to show up before those risks become more serious? Those early indicators can become the signals your team tracks more closely.

Using Sprout Social Listening, the Atlas team tracks these patterns across channels and spots connections that might be easy to miss when looking at each account on its own. From there, the team can then investigate what’s happening and decide whether a local market needs more guidance.

2. Establish a clear governance framework

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Those shared expectations also strengthen brand safety. When multiple teams and contributors manage social accounts, clear ownership and review processes create more consistency around how teams publish content and respond to potential issues.

Atlas Copco Group uses Tagging in Sprout to organize content by quality and compliance, track which teams are meeting brand standards and identify where additional support is needed.

3. Standardize account health metrics

Atlas Copco Group uses a consistent set of metrics to evaluate brand health in various markets. The team looks at activity, brand compliance, response times and audience engagement together to create a more objective view of performance.

articles.title: How to use social listening and media monitoring for corporate reputation management
articles.fullContent:
You spend years managing a vibrant, positive brand reputation—nailing the customer experience, delivering great service and watching your reputation thrive. But all it takes is one viral post to make that hard work feel like it’s disappearing overnight.

Even the most experienced marketers face this reality. According to an Axios Harris Poll, 46% of corporate reputations have declined between 2019 and 2025.

Managing brand sentiment can feel overwhelming, but you can take control of your brand’s narrative with a smart corporate reputation management strategy.

What is corporate reputation management?

Corporate reputation management is the practice of proactively influencing and maintaining how the public perceives your brand. This includes monitoring conversations about your company, resolving issues quickly and amplifying positive moments to shape your brand perception.

Corporate reputation management and online reputation management go hand-in-hand. For modern brands, the key aspect that sets them apart is the online focus, which highlights how digital conversations unfolding online shape brand perception and how customers expect you to actively listen on social.

According to a Q2 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, consumers say social is the number one place they hear about a brand crisis first. And when a crisis happens, 64% of consumers say it’s important for a brand to respond publicly on social media rather than through a press release or website statement. This is why social media teams are on the front lines, tasked with protecting and nurturing brand reputation.

A great example of managing a ‘crisis’ online—and getting ahead of the conversation— is the 2018 #ChickenCrises. When KFC ran out of chicken and had to shut down over 750 stores, customers were not happy. Using social listening, the brand noticed the backlash brewing online and quickly addressed the issue with an edgy, self-aware response. They rearranged the letters “KFC” on a chicken bucket to look like a curse word, essentially saying: “We messed up.”

This light-hearted, authentic response defused tension, protected the brand’s reputation and sparked viral trends. And there’s a reason we’re still talking about it eight years later: it’s become an iconic example of a brand apology. It reinforces how vital it is for social media professionals to listen, engage and collaborate with stakeholders to manage reputation challenges to shape brand perception.

Trust impacts everyone from consumers to investors (63% cite it as a critical factor in business-related decisions, according to the Phillips Group). As a marketing leader, your opportunity is to proactively build and protect corporate reputation by engaging with audience conversations and influencing your company’s narrative, wherever it happens.

Why corporate reputation management is important today

Your reputation shapes every part of your business, from winning stakeholder trust to driving sales and building customer loyalty. Because reputation is foundational to brand health, damage to it is one of the biggest risks companies face today.

In highly regulated sectors like financial services, social media acts as an early warning system; a single misunderstood fee structure or service outage can escalate into a compliance nightmare if not addressed with immediate, transparent communication.

The classic Harvard Business Review’s Reputation and Its Risks, notes that 70-80% of the modern economy’s market value comes from “hard-to-assess intangible assets,” like brand equity. This means anything that can hinder your brand—a bad reputation, a crisis—has the power to affect your entire business. Modern data confirms this: Aon’s findings rank reputation damage as the eighth biggest risk to companies worldwide.

But even when you do everything right, outside factors may still influence your reputation. In 2025, a user on Reddit reported that GameStop had charged customers for unreceived products following a $1.4 million merchandise heist.

Rather than letting the issue escalate, GameStop’s social media team acted quickly with a proactive response that clarified that no customer orders were affected. This action helped the company protect its reputation and maintain brand trust.

Source: Reddit

GameStop’s social media response made the difference between protecting its reputation and letting a false story spread unchecked. Their social team listened, researched the facts and responded quickly with clarity.

By spotting issues early and responding quickly, your company reduces the impact of negative reputation events. But reputation management is more than avoiding the negative. As a marketer, you also have the ability to proactively nurture your brand perception online to get ahead of risk, too.

Take Atlas Copco group as an example. The organization uses social listening and intelligence to identify sentiment and trends online, and to address small issues before they become brand risks. The team saw that many risks don’t start as large spikes. They show up first as small, repeatable instances like questions, inconsistencies in activity or brand content, and even how local markets experience the brand differently. Each little concern doesn’t seem alarming, but when stacked together, the brand risks start to become clear.

Understanding these patterns through regular listening led them to use social data to push for increased training and governance for internal teams, so they could address inconsistencies early and act before the small moments escalated into larger reputation concerns.

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.

Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.

But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.

Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.

Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.

According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.

But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.

Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.

The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.

For example:

  • Tease what’s coming: Preview holiday collections, seasonal launches or upcoming offers.
  • Get gift-worthy products on shoppers’ radar: Introduce products consumers might want to add to their lists before they’re ready to buy.
  • Start publishing seasonal content: Share gift inspiration and other useful holiday content that gives shoppers a reason to engage early.

Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.

Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.

Timing also depends on who you’re trying to reach. Younger consumers are especially receptive to an early start: 66% of Gen Z consumers say campaigns launching as early as August make them more likely to buy, compared to 49% of consumers overall.

Tariffs and price pressure are reshaping purchase patterns

Many consumers see shopping earlier as a way to get ahead of rising prices. More than a third (36%) say they’re starting their holiday shopping earlier specifically to avoid tariff-related price increases. Another 27% aren’t shopping earlier yet but are concerned about prices.

In total, 63% of holiday shoppers are thinking about the impact of higher prices.

Those concerns are also affecting how much consumers plan to spend. More than half (56%) expect to reduce their holiday spending this year because of economic conditions like tariffs and the cost of living. Only 30% say they don’t plan to cut back.

Price sensitivity doesn’t mean every brand needs to compete on having the lowest price. Shoppers may be looking more closely at what they get for their money, so holiday content should make value clear. Highlight product quality, versatility or other details that make a purchase feel worthwhile.

Discounts can also tip the scales: Promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top purchase driver, cited by 30% of consumers. Lastly, brands with products at multiple price points can also organize gift recommendations by budget, making it easier for shoppers to find options that work for them.

For example, last holiday season, REI shared a roundup of expert picks under $50 on Instagram, with a CTA to check out their larger holiday gift guide.

Consumers are discovering gifts on social this year

Social media now rivals in-store shopping for holiday gift discovery. This year, 46% of consumers say they’ll turn to social for gift ideas and product discovery—the same percentage who plan to browse physical stores.

Where consumers turn for holiday gift ideas:

  • Social media: 46%
  • Physical stores: 46%
  • Recommendations from friends and family: 34%
  • TV: 31%
  • Review sites: 23%
  • AI chatbots: 15%

And social’s influence is still growing. Compared to the 2025 holiday season, 28% of consumers plan to use social more to find gifts this year, while another 50% expect their usage to stay about the same.

That creates an opportunity to reach shoppers before they know exactly what they want to buy.

Think about how easily someone encountering your brand for the first time can understand what you sell, who your products are for and why they’re worth considering. Content organized around recipients, interests, occasions or price points can make that discovery process easier and give shoppers a reason to explore your products further.

Bookshop.org, for example, used Instagram to promote its 2025 holiday gift guide, which curated hundreds of recommendations for different types of readers and paired them with a limited-time discount.

What drives a purchase on social?

Discovery is only the first step. Once shoppers find a product on social, the content surrounding it can influence whether they buy.

According to the Q3 2026 pulse survey, promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top social-specific purchase trigger at 30%, followed closely by brand posts showing products in action at 28%. Original holiday content from brands influences 26% of consumers, while 22% point to content from non-influencer users.

For years, public relations and SEO have operated in neighboring but often separate parts of the marketing organization. AI search is beginning to change that relationship.

As AI systems become a larger part of how people discover companies, products, and services, the sources those systems rely on are becoming increasingly important. Third-party coverage from trusted publications can provide information that helps establish a brand’s credibility and authority.
That shift is changing how organizations think about digital PR.
New industry projections suggest PR budgets could double by 2027 as brands respond to the growing importance of AI-powered search. The underlying reason is straightforward: brands need to be visible in the places AI systems use to understand and evaluate them.
For marketers, that makes earned media more than a traditional awareness channel. Consistent third-party coverage can contribute to a brand’s broader search presence while strengthening the information available about it across the web.

Why AI Search Is Increasing the Value of Digital PR

AI search changes how people encounter information. Instead of receiving a list of links and deciding which ones to visit, users can receive a synthesized answer based on information gathered from multiple sources.

That creates a new role for third-party coverage.

AI Systems Rely on Trusted Sources

AI systems need information they can retrieve and use when generating answers.

A company’s own website is an important source, but it isn’t the only one. News publications, industry websites, reviews, research organizations, and other third-party sources can provide additional context about a brand. Academic databases are a great example.

This is where earned media becomes valuable.

A company that is consistently mentioned by credible publications creates a broader information footprint than one that relies primarily on its own website. Those mentions can help reinforce what the company does, who its experts are, and where it has authority.

That doesn’t guarantee an AI system will cite any particular article. It does create more opportunities for a brand’s information to exist within the sources AI systems may encounter.

Authority is difficult to establish through a single piece of coverage.

One major publication can create awareness, but its effect can fade. A sustained presence across relevant publications creates a different type of signal.

Repeated coverage can reinforce the same core facts about a business across multiple sources. Over time, this can contribute to stronger brand recognition and a clearer understanding of the company’s expertise.

For AI visibility, that consistency matters because AI systems are constantly processing information from across the web.

Why One Media Win Isn’t Enough

The temptation in PR has often been to measure success by the biggest placement a campaign can generate. A marquee publication can certainly be valuable, but it shouldn’t be the only objective.

Credibility Compounds Over Time

A single article can introduce a company to a new audience. An ongoing stream of relevant coverage can keep reinforcing the brand.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within seven days, according to Similarweb research.
  • Most AI-influenced visits did not arrive through an identifiable AI referral.
  • More than half of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, meaning the AI influence can look like ordinary organic traffic in analytics.
  • Last-click attribution can therefore underestimate the role AI plays in brand discovery and consideration.
  • Marketers need broader measurement frameworks that account for AI’s influence across the customer journey.

AI search is becoming an increasingly important way for consumers to discover brands. But measuring its impact is proving much harder than measuring a traditional referral.

A user might ask ChatGPT for a product recommendation, see a brand mentioned, and then search for that brand on Google several days later. Analytics will record the eventual visit, but it may have no way of knowing that an AI recommendation helped start the journey.

New research from Similarweb highlights the scale of this measurement gap. Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within the following seven days, even when there was no direct referral from the AI platform.

The finding suggests that AI visibility can influence traffic without appearing as AI traffic in a standard analytics report.

For marketers, that’s an important distinction. If AI is influencing customers before they reach a website, measuring only the final click can make the channel look less valuable than it actually is.

What Similarweb Found About AI’s Downstream Impact

Similarweb’s research tracked real user journeys to understand what happens after a brand is recommended in ChatGPT.

Source

AI Recommendations Can Lead to More Website Visits</h3>

Similarweb followed users who asked ChatGPT an industry-related question and received a specific brand recommendation. It then tracked their behavior over the following seven days.

Across finance, travel, and beauty, users who received an AI recommendation for a brand were 2.5x more likely to visit that brand’s website than users who received a recommendation for a competing brand.

The research focused on users who had not previously visited the recommended brand and had not already mentioned that brand in their prompt. This helped Similarweb measure the downstream effect of a recommendation rather than simply tracking people who already knew about a company.

The result provides a useful signal for marketers investing in AI visibility. Being mentioned in an AI answer can influence what consumers do afterward, even when the AI platform doesn’t send the eventual website visit.

Most of the Traffic Doesn’t Look Like AI Traffic

This is where traditional measurement becomes complicated.

Similarweb found that 55.9% of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, compared with 40.4% of visits without AI influence.

In practice, that means a user could see a brand recommendation in ChatGPT, remember the name, and later search for it on Google.

That visit would likely be attributed to organic search.

The AI interaction that helped create the interest would receive no credit.

This is the core AI attribution problem. The measurable traffic is real, but the original source of influence can disappear somewhere between discovery and conversion.

Source

Why Last-Click Attribution Misses AI’s Influence

Last-click attribution works reasonably well when a customer journey is relatively direct. But discovery through AI can introduce additional steps that aren’t captured by traditional referral reporting.

The AI Interaction Happens Before the Measurable Visit

Consider a simple journey.

A consumer asks an AI platform which software tools are best for their business. The platform recommends a brand. The consumer doesn’t click a link. Instead, they continue researching, then return to Google two days later and search for the brand by name.

From an analytics perspective, the final visit may look like a branded organic search.

From the customer’s perspective, however, the journey started with AI.
